extDescription.message: Stamps every outgoing message with PasevSU forensic headers, a SHA-256 evidence chain and PasevSU_Manifest.json.

optionsIntro.message: These values are written into every outgoing email as X-PasevSU-* headers. Changes apply from the next message you send.

armedChecking.message: Checking whether the background script is armed…

armedNoReport.message: Not armed — the background script has not reported yet. Restart Thunderbird.

manifestError.message: Last send: the manifest could NOT be attached — $reason$

lastSendSummary.message: Stamped $count$ message(s). Last: $when$, Evidence-ID $evidence$, $files$ attachment(s), $headers$ headers.

lastSendNone.message: Stamped 0 messages — no outgoing message has been stamped yet. Send one and this line will update.

attachmentHashes.message: Attachment hashes in the last message:

attachmentFailures.message: Attachments that could not be read (named in X-PasevSU-Attachments-Error): $list$

receiptError.message: No receipt address: the receipt header is only written when the sending identity or the fallback address below is known.

fingerprintInvalid.message: The fingerprint was not saved: it must be 40 or 64 hexadecimal characters (no spaces). Copy it from the key properties in Thunderbird.

fingerprintIsKeyId.message: That is a key ID (8 or 16 characters), not a fingerprint. Open the key properties and copy the full 40-character fingerprint.

rejectedHeaders.message: Headers the extension refused to write (only X-, List- and msip_labels names are allowed): $list$

fingerprintIssueNotHex.message: Recorded at $at$: the PGP fingerprint contains characters other than 0-9 and A-F, so no PGP claim was written.

fingerprintIssueKeyId.message: Recorded at $at$: the PGP fingerprint field holds a key ID, not a fingerprint, so no PGP claim was written.

fingerprintIssueWrongLength.message: Recorded at $at$: the PGP fingerprint is neither 40 nor 64 hexadecimal characters, so no PGP claim was written.

restampReasonEvidenceHeader.message: the evidence header was already in the message

restampsSummary.message: A send pass re-ran $count$ time(s) without stamping again. Last: $when$ — $reason$.

caseIdHint.message: e.g. CASE-2026-001 (leave empty to omit the header)

pgpHint.message: e.g. 3F2A9C… (leave empty to omit the header)

labelPgpSigner.message: PGP signer address (named in the WAR notice)

pgpSignerHint.message: e.g. name@example.org (leave empty to use the shipped default)

labelPgpStandard.message: Signature standard named in the WAR notice

labelOts.message: Mark every message for OpenTimestamps (X-PasevSU-OTS: pending)

labelReceipt.message: Request a read receipt on every message (Thunderbird adds Disposition-Notification-To)

labelDeliveryReceipt.message: Request a delivery receipt on every message (Thunderbird adds the DSN fields, RFC 3461)

labelReceiptMode.message: Where the receipt address comes from

receiptModeIdentity.message: The sending identity from the profile

receiptModeHint.message: the profile is read on every send, so a new account needs no new setting

receiptAddressHint.message: only used when Thunderbird does not report the sending identity

evidenceChainNote.message: These names are written into the hashed manifest and into every verification instruction, so a second deployment can say who minted a message without changing code.

messageIdDomainHint.message: the right-hand side of the Message-ID; the local part is derived from the evidence id

manifestFilenameHint.message: the attachment name and the name every verification step refers to

labelManifestFramework.message: Framework word written in the manifest

manifestFrameworkHint.message: inside the hashed manifest; a verifier cuts on this name

labelManifestStandard.message: Standard word written in the manifest

manifestStandardHint.message: names the protocol the package follows, e.g. PSEMP

algoBodyHint.message: the hash the manifest publishes for the message body

algoExtraHint.message: comma-separated, published as a list; leave empty for no extra hashes

algoMerkleHint.message: the hash used for the evidence tree

algoEngineHint.message: the cipher named for the encrypted digest block

algoSignatureHint.message: e.g. OpenPGP; recorded, not performed by the extension

algoTimestampHint.message: e.g. OpenTimestamps; recorded, not performed by the extension

sharedIntro.message: The gateway keeps the same keys in psemp-gateway/settings.default.json. Import it here so both halves agree on version, framework, organization and PGP fingerprint, and export the current values back to that file when you change them.

originNote.message: origin is not copied from the file: it names the producer, so the extension always writes Thunderbird and the gateway writes PSEMP-Gateway. That is the only intentional difference between the two, and the parity test asserts it.

pgpNote.message: OpenPGP already configured in Thunderbird. Put the fingerprint of the key your account already signs with here (Account Settings → End-to-End Encryption → OpenPGP Key Manager → your key). A MailExtension cannot read Thunderbird's keyring, so this header is a claim: it is the one value a recipient has to check against the signature. psemp-gateway pgp-check compares the claim with the signer actually present in the delivered message, and it never adds a second signature to a message Thunderbird already signed. Thunderbird signs PGP/MIME with protected-headers="v1", so the X-PasevSU-* headers are repeated inside the signed part and editing one breaks the signature — but with encryption switched on the headers stay in the clear while the body does not.

limitationsNote.message: Real OpenPGP signatures (.asc) and OpenTimestamps (.ots) cannot be produced inside a Thunderbird MailExtension; the X-PasevSU-OTS header is a marker for the SMTP gateway. Run node psemp-gateway/cli.js seal PasevSU_Manifest.json to turn the marker into a real detached signature and proof. The marker is written by default so no message is ever sent unstamped — untick the box only if you deliberately do not want the gateway to seal.

receiptNote.message: Two different requests. The read receipt is standard MDN (RFC 8098): the recipient is asked, not obliged, and most clients show a dialog — Thunderbird's own Return Receipts setting in Account Settings asks as well, and both may appear, which is harmless. The delivery receipt is standard DSN (RFC 3461): the receiving server reports delivery or failure and the recipient is never asked. Both go to the address the message is sent from.
